title: Existence of consistent hypo- and hyperresponders to dietary cholesterol in man
authors: Katan MB, Beynen AC, de Vries JH, Nobels A
followUp: Three controlled feeding experiments in 1982, each a low-cholesterol period followed by a high-cholesterol period of 13 to 28 days
population: Healthy volunteers living in or near Wageningen, the Netherlands
funder: Supported by the Netherlands Heart Foundation, grants no. 31.013, 78.093, 79.045 and 26.003. M. B. Katan is an established investigator of the Netherlands Heart Foundation.
inKindSupport: The methods name a special bread from Crock-Laan and a special margarine from Van den Bergh & Jurgens B.V.; the paper does not state whether they were donated.
result: Egg yolk supplied the added cholesterol, the only dietary variable. In experiment 1, 94 adults whose intake rose from 121 to 625 mg/day showed a rise in serum cholesterol of 0.50 ± 0.39 mmol/L. Seventeen putative hyperresponders and 15 hyporesponders selected in experiment 1 showed responses of 0.28 ± 0.38 and 0.06 ± 0.35 mmol/L in experiment 2 (106 to 673 mg/day) and 0.82 ± 0.35 and 0.47 ± 0.26 mmol/L in experiment 3 (129 to 989 mg/day). After correction for within-person fluctuation, the between-subject standard deviation of true responsiveness was about 0.29 mmol/L; mean individual responses formed a unimodal distribution without discrete subgroups. The authors conclude that modest differences in responsiveness exist and that the wide scatter of responses in single experiments is largely due to chance fluctuations.
